title: Beyond Good and Evil
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
openingText: Supposing that Truth is a woman — what then? Is there not ground for suspecting that all philosophers, in so far as they have been dogmatists, have failed to understand women — that the terrible seriousness and clumsy importunity with which they have usually paid their addresses to Truth, have been unskilled and unseemly methods for winning a woman? Certainly she has never allowed herself to be won; and at present every kind of dogma stands with sad and discouraged mien — if, indeed, it stands at all! For there are scoffers who maintain that it has fallen, that all dogma lies on the ground — nay more, that it is at its last gasp.
about:
Beyond Good and Evil is Nietzsche's attempt to think past the inherited categories of Western morality. Across nine chapters and 296 numbered sections, he attacks the pretensions of philosophers, the nature of truth, the morality of priests, the difference between "noble" and "slave" moralities, and the prospects for free spirits able to create new values. The book is aphoristic, polemical, and often deliberately provocative.

Nietzsche published it in 1886, a few years before his collapse into madness. It is the most accessible of his major works — short, propulsive, and direct — and the place most readers begin. It is also the work that most directly raises the questions that 20th-century philosophy spent a century trying to answer.

angleCards.title: The will to power as the hidden engine of morality.
angleCards.text: Every moral system, Nietzsche argues, is a disguised bid for dominance — a way of making your instincts into law, your preferences into virtue. Read BGE asking who gains from each moral claim: the priest, the herd, the philosopher, the slave. The answer is never who it appears to be.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Beyond Good and Evil as an exposé of power — tracking how moral language conceals the will to dominate beneath the vocabulary of goodness, duty, and truth.

angleCards.title: Master morality vs. slave morality.
angleCards.text: Nietzsche draws a sharp line between two kinds of ethical world-making: the noble who defines good from strength and then names its opposite as bad, and the resentful who defines evil first — as what oppresses them — and then calls its negation good. Christianity, democracy, and socialism are all, for Nietzsche, slave-morality in disguise.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Nietzsche's distinction between master and slave morality through the text — identifying where modern values fall on that axis and what it would mean to live beyond both.

angleCards.title: Nietzsche's attack on the prejudices of philosophers.
angleCards.text: Part One is a sustained demolition of the assumption that philosophers seek truth. Nietzsche argues they seek confirmation — that every great system is an autobiography dressed in logic, a personal drive disguised as universal reason. Reading this way turns the history of philosophy into a psychology of its authors.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read BGE as a critique of how philosophy works — what it actually does versus what it claims to do, and what that reveals about Kant, Plato, Schopenhauer, and the rest.

angleCards.title: The free spirit as the book's quiet hero.
angleCards.text: BGE is not only destruction. Threading through the attacks is a portrait of a different kind of person: the free spirit, who has escaped the comfort of inherited values, who tolerates uncertainty without fleeing into dogma, and who experiments rather than obeys. Nietzsche means this as an aspiration, not just a description.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read BGE for its positive vision — what kind of person survives the collapse of traditional morality, and whether Nietzsche's free spirit is actually liveable or just a gesture toward something he cannot quite name.

cast.name: Will to Power
cast.description: Not a desire for political domination but the fundamental tendency of all life to expand, create, and impose its own form on the world. Nietzsche argues that this is the real engine beneath every human instinct — including the instinct for truth, pity, and self-sacrifice.

cast.name: Master Morality
cast.description: The ethics of strength: the noble type defines "good" from its own excellence and names its opposite "bad" as an afterthought. It is creative, forward-looking, and indifferent to the suffering it leaves behind. Nietzsche traces it to the aristocratic cultures of antiquity.

cast.name: Slave Morality
cast.description: The ethics of the oppressed: it begins with hatred of the strong, names that strength "evil," and then declares its own weakness virtuous. Christianity is its supreme expression. Nietzsche does not dismiss it as simply false — he calls it one of history's most creative inversions.

cast.name: The Free Spirit
cast.description: Nietzsche's portrait of the philosopher who has passed beyond inherited morality without falling into nihilism. The free spirit is hard on itself, comfortable with uncertainty, and tests ideas by living them rather than by submitting them to logical proof. BGE is partly written for this person and partly written to create them.

cast.name: Perspectivism
cast.description: There is no view from nowhere. Every claim about truth, Nietzsche argues, is made from a position — a body, an instinct, a historical moment — and cannot escape it. This does not mean all views are equal; it means the honesty of a view depends on acknowledging what it owes to its origin.

cast.name: Herd Morality
cast.description: The moral code of the majority, which values safety, uniformity, and the suppression of the exceptional. Nietzsche sees modern democracy, European Christianity, and utilitarian ethics as three faces of the same herd instinct — all enforcing conformity under different names.

whyItMatters.title: Beyond the Inherited Map
whyItMatters.body: The book takes the moral categories Western thought had inherited from Plato and Christianity — good and evil, truth and lie, virtue and vice — and asks whether they make sense. Nietzsche's argument is that they do not, and that the work of modern thought is figuring out what to put in their place.

whyItMatters.title: The Genealogy of Truth
whyItMatters.body: Nietzsche treats philosophical claims as expressions of the philosopher's psychology, not as discoveries of objective truth. The move was new in 1886 and remains contested. It is the source of the modern habit of asking, "What's really going on with this argument?"

whyItMatters.title: The Aphoristic Form
whyItMatters.body: The book is organized in short numbered sections — some a sentence long, some a few pages. Nietzsche believed long systematic prose hid more than it showed. The form makes the reader work, reread, sit with paradoxes. It is a philosophical strategy, not just a stylistic choice.
